- When sentiment is strongly positive (e.g., >0.3) and forecast is rising sharply, reduce peak overshoots by 5–10% to avoid overreacting to sentiment.
- When sentiment is strongly negative (e.g., < -0.3) and forecast is falling, avoid premature bottoming — delay downward correction by 1–2 periods to allow for mean reversion.
- If recent history shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days of price decline after a spike), model should not overcorrect downward; instead, slightly bias forecast upward to avoid “overbought” traps.
- For 30-day forecasts, if sentiment is volatile or mixed (e.g., alternating +/–0.2), reduce forecast volatility — smooth out sharp swings to avoid overfitting to short-term sentiment noise.
- If forecast consistently overestimates true price after a spike (e.g., +10%+ above true), apply a “cooling-off” rule: subtract 2–3% from peak forecast values if sentiment is neutral or slightly negative.
- When sentiment is consistently positive over 3+ days, model should not assume continuation — instead, slightly dampen upward trend to account for potential exhaustion or policy intervention.
